text: One solid shape.
It can fill three-dimensional space.

Yet none of its tilings repeats by translation.
Meet Chair44 (R44).
First, remove its tiny surface features.
What remains is a chair made from seven cubes.
This plain chair also fills space.

Slide the outlined strip by this vector.
It lands on identical chairs.
The same translation works again. And again.

One repeating tiling is enough:
this chair is not an aperiodic monotile.
Now restore Chair44’s 192 tiny bumps and dents.

These bumps and dents change
which placements fit together.

Keep the chairs in that repeating arrangement.
These copies now overlap.

So that arrangement fails.
But ruling out one arrangement is not enough.
Can Chair44 fill space at all?

Yes. Here are actual copies
in compatible positions.

Eight copies form a cluster
shaped like a doubled plain chair.

Larger compatible patches grow
around a fixed tile.

The construction extends to fill all of space.
The screen shows only a finite part.

Every copy is the same shape.
Colours only help us follow the construction.

The claim concerns every tiling of Chair44—
not just the one being built here.

Local patterns can recur.
The whole tiling cannot repeat by translation.
Why? The geometry forces a unique hierarchy.

Chairs group into larger chairs,
then larger chairs again.

The proof recovers a valid Chair44 tiling
after each grouping and rescaling.

A translation period would survive each step,
with its vector halved every time.

At every level a period has integer coordinates
in that level’s registered unit grid.

Only the zero vector can keep being halved
and still have integer coordinates forever.

Rotations and reflections were allowed.
No colouring or matching rules were imposed.

Even so, a tiling cannot mix the tile
with its mirror image.

Every tiling has at most 24 symmetries.
None is a screw motion with a nonzero slide.

One connected solid. Shape alone.
An aperiodic monotile in three dimensions.

Explore the tile. Run the notebook.
Ask your own AI to check the proof.
